title: The HALO Trust trains AI, supported by Amazon Web Services, to find explosive remnants in drone imagery of Ukrainian minefields; it reaches about 70% accuracy, and no clearance outcome is attributed to it
summary: The HALO Trust's AI detects mines in drone imagery of Ukrainian minefields with about 70% accuracy, and HALO says that it cuts analysis from days to hours; no cleared land is attributed to it.
account: The HALO Trust announced a US$4 million package of support from Amazon Web Services on 25 June 2024. An archived copy of the page, dated 20 May 2026, is among the sources. The package “will enable HALO to trial artificial intelligence (AI) to assist in the process of detecting debris of war (including landmines and other explosives) in drone imagery for existing minefields and battlefields in Ukraine”. It also covers machine-learning detection of damaged buildings in satellite imagery with SageMaker. By then HALO had flown 542 drone flights over Ukrainian minefields, producing 11 terabytes of imagery. HALO said that training would require manually labeling thousands of images and ongoing vetting by HALO staff to remove false positives and negatives. A HALO page of 21 February 2025 describes the pilot through its head of research and development, Matthew Abercrombie. He says that an analyst “can take three to five days to look through the imagery for an average minefield”. The page reports no results. On 24 April 2026 HALO wrote that Prince Harry had flown an AI-powered drone at one of its sites near Bucha. HALO said that its AI models now analyze terrain in hours where manual assessments took days, and it gave no measured figure. Reuters (Sergiy Karazy, 30 April 2026, syndicated by KELO) reported from Myrotske, 40 km northwest of Kyiv. It reported that HALO “has turned to AI to analyse high-resolution drone imagery of contaminated areas and train systems to identify mines and explosive remnants, achieving around 70% accuracy already”. It quoted HALO media manager Olena Shustova. The article does not mention Amazon Web Services, and it attributes no cleared land, found mine or time saving to the model. No later milestone is dated.
purpose: Built to flag landmines and other debris of war in drone imagery so that HALO analysts spend less time searching thousands of images per minefield. The pilot is that intended use.
system: HALO Trust AI and machine-learning analysis of drone imagery for explosive remnants of war (hosted on AWS; SageMaker used for satellite-imagery damage detection)

The Reuters report of 30 April 2026, syndicated by KELO, is the only independent source, and it gives the figure of about 70% accuracy.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: The HALO Trust's AI detects mines in drone imagery of Ukrainian minefields with about 70% accuracy, and HALO says that it cuts analysis from days to hours; no cleared land is attributed to it.
fields.account: The HALO Trust announced a US$4 million package of support from Amazon Web Services on 25 June 2024. An archived copy of the page, dated 20 May 2026, is among the sources. The package “will enable HALO to trial artificial intelligence (AI) to assist in the process of detecting debris of war (including landmines and other explosives) in drone imagery for existing minefields and battlefields in Ukraine”. It also covers machine-learning detection of damaged buildings in satellite imagery with SageMaker. By then HALO had flown 542 drone flights over Ukrainian minefields, producing 11 terabytes of imagery. HALO said that training would require manually labeling thousands of images and ongoing vetting by HALO staff to remove false positives and negatives. A HALO page of 21 February 2025 describes the pilot through its head of research and development, Matthew Abercrombie. He says that an analyst “can take three to five days to look through the imagery for an average minefield”. The page reports no results. On 24 April 2026 HALO wrote that Prince Harry had flown an AI-powered drone at one of its sites near Bucha. HALO said that its AI models now analyze terrain in hours where manual assessments took days, and it gave no measured figure. Reuters (Sergiy Karazy, 30 April 2026, syndicated by KELO) reported from Myrotske, 40 km northwest of Kyiv. It reported that HALO “has turned to AI to analyse high-resolution drone imagery of contaminated areas and train systems to identify mines and explosive remnants, achieving around 70% accuracy already”. It quoted HALO media manager Olena Shustova. The article does not mention Amazon Web Services, and it attributes no cleared land, found mine or time saving to the model. No later milestone is dated.
